scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Chinelos dance originated in the 19th century in Morelos, Mexico, particularly in Tlayacapan.
It arose as a form of social satire by indigenous laborers who mocked European colonialists and hacendados during Carnival, a festival allowing masked role reversal and social critique.
The name derives from the Nahuatl word "zineloquie," meaning "disguised." The dance developed amid the harsh conditions of sugarcane haciendas, where workers were impoverished and exploited.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Chinelos traditionally perform during Carnival, from late January to the start of Lent, in towns across Morelos and parts of Mexico City and the State of Mexico.
They also appear at Independence Day celebrations and private parties.
The dance is a form of social satire mocking colonial authorities and hacendados who exploited indigenous laborers.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The costume consists of a long flowing velvet robe with a rectangular tunic shape, a large feathered hat, a mesh mask with an upturned beard and European features, and white gloves.
The robes give an androgynous appearance.
Costumes are elaborately decorated with beads, sequins, and imitation jewels, varying by town.

scenes.title: The people
narration: José Salazar Flores of Tepotzlán is a noted maker of Chinelo hats, dedicating his livelihood to crafting these elaborate pieces.
The Banda de Música Santa María de Tlayacapan is the most famous musical group associated with the tradition.

Distinctive costume styles exist in different towns: Tlayacapan's costume is closest to the original 19th-century form with a broader, less embellished hat and a white or blue tunic with an image of the Virgin of Guadalupe.
Chinelos evolved from indigenous and Catholic traditions blending after the Spanish conquest, particularly Carnival's customs of masking and social inversion.

wardrobe.from_sources: The costume consists of a long flowing velvet robe with a rectangular tunic shape, a large feathered hat, a mesh mask with an upturned beard and European features, and white gloves. The robes give an androgynous appearance. Costumes are elaborately decorated with beads, sequins, and imitation jewels, varying by town. The hat is made of fabric with a palm leaf frame and decorated with feathers and pre-Hispanic motifs. Costumes are expensive and closely guarded to preserve anonymity. Dancers wear bandanas under hats to absorb sweat. Performances occur outdoors during Carnival and other festivals, often in town plazas or monastery atriums.

visual_brief.costume_notes: The costume consists of a long flowing velvet robe with a rectangular tunic shape, a large feathered hat, a mesh mask with an upturned beard and European features, and white gloves. The robes give an androgynous appearance. Costumes are elaborately decorated with beads, sequins, and imitation jewels, varying by town. The hat is made of fabric with a palm leaf frame and decorated with feathers and pre-Hispanic motifs. Costumes are expensive and closely guarded to preserve anonymity. Dancers wear bandanas under hats to absorb sweat. Performances occur outdoors during Carnival and other festivals, often in town plazas or monastery atriums.
visual_brief.setting_notes: Chinelos traditionally perform during Carnival, from late January to the start of Lent, in towns across Morelos and parts of Mexico City and the State of Mexico. They also appear at Independence Day celebrations and private parties. The dance is a form of social satire mocking colonial authorities and hacendados who exploited indigenous laborers. It symbolizes cultural resistance and identity. The tradition is passed down within families, often from father to son. The dance is a highlight of Carnival festivities, drawing large crowds and fostering community pride.
